sections.heading: Polarity values
sections.text: AMI is a bipolar line code. A zero bit (space) is always a zero voltage level. A one bit (mark) is either +1 or -1, and the polarity of a one alternates from one mark to the next. The very first mark in a stream is +1.

sections.heading: Zeros never reset polarity
sections.text: A run of zeros does NOT reset the alternation. The polarity continues alternating through zero bits, so a student who assumes a run of zeros flips the mark back to +1 is misreading the signal.

sections.heading: DC component
sections.text: Because +1 and -1 marks alternate, AMI has a near-zero DC component. A measured DC offset is a quick check that the encoder is not producing unipolar NRZ (which holds one level and carries a large DC offset).

sections.heading: Transitions
sections.text: AMI has no guaranteed transitions at every bit boundary when zeros are present: a zero bit has no transition (both samples are 0). Transitions appear only at marks.

sections.heading: Transition every bit period
sections.text: Manchester encoding guarantees a mid-bit transition for every bit period, which makes it self-clocking. The data bit is carried by the direction of the transition, not by the absolute level.

sections.heading: IEEE 802.3 convention
sections.text: Under the IEEE 802.3 convention (the one used by this lab): a 1 is low-then-high (level drops then rises in the middle of the bit), and a 0 is high-then-low. The opposite mapping (G. E. Thomas) appears in some textbooks, a common source of waveform inversion.

sections.heading: Sampling at two per bit
sections.text: Manchester requires at least two samples per bit so the mid-bit transition lands between samples. With only one sample per bit the signal would look like plain NRZ, which is the classic student error.

sections.heading: NRZ-L (polar, level based)
sections.text: NRZ-L maps a 1 to a positive level (+1) and a 0 to a negative level (-1), and holds that level for the whole bit period. It is level-based and has no transitions at bit boundaries unless the level changes.

sections.heading: Unipolar NRZ
sections.text: Unipolar NRZ uses only one polarity: a 1 is +1 and a 0 is 0. Because only one level is used, unipolar NRZ has a large DC component. Do not confuse it with polar NRZ-L, which uses both +1 and -1.

sections.heading: What a student should watch for
sections.text: NRZ-L is level-based, not transition-based. If a student treats it like NRZ-I (inverted), where a 1 causes the level to flip at the boundary, the waveform will be wrong even though the bits are the same. The key check is the level, not the edge.

sections.heading: Pulse shape
sections.text: Unipolar RZ sends a positive pulse for the first half of the bit period and then returns to 0 for the second half. A 0 stays at zero for the entire bit period. The return to zero inside the bit period makes RZ self-clocking.

sections.heading: Sampling
sections.text: RZ needs an even number of samples per bit so the mid-bit return to zero is represented exactly. One sample per bit collapses RZ into plain NRZ, which is the most common waveform mismatch in this lab.

sections.heading: Why line coding matters
sections.text: A line-coded waveform carries raw bits across a wire. The transmitter maps each bit to a voltage pattern, and the receiver must be able to recover the clock and the bits from that pattern.

sections.heading: Four properties to compare
sections.text: When a student reads a waveform they should check four things: (1) the logic levels used (+1/-1/0), (2) whether transitions are guaranteed at every bit boundary, (3) the DC component of the stream, and (4) whether the code is self-clocking.

sections.heading: Wiring to the encoder
sections.text: The bit source has a single output (source.out) wired to the encoder input (encoder.in). The encoder output (encoder.out) feeds the oscilloscope (scope.in). A circuit missing the source-to-encoder wire, or missing the encoder-to-scope wire, is incomplete.

sections.heading: AMI polarity reset after zeros
sections.text: Assuming a run of zeros resets mark polarity. AMI alternates across the whole stream regardless of intervening zeros. This is the top AMI fault in the kit.

sections.heading: NRZ-L / NRZ-I confusion
sections.text: Treating NRZ-L as transition-based. NRZ-L is level-based; NRZ-I encodes by a transition at the bit boundary. The same bits give different waveforms.

sections.heading: Manchester convention flip
sections.text: Using the G. E. Thomas mapping (1 = high-then-low) where IEEE 802.3 (1 = low-then-high) is expected. The waveform is the exact inverse.

sections.heading: Reading the scope trace
sections.text: Each bit occupies samples_per_bit samples. The oscilloscope plots the sampled voltage. Compare the shape against the known pattern of the chosen code, and read the DC component and transition count on the stats panel.

sections.heading: DC component
sections.text: DC component is the mean level of the waveform. Codes that alternate +1 and -1 (AMI) sit near zero; codes that stay near one level (unipolar NRZ) have a large DC offset. Compare against the stats panel to confirm the code.

sections.heading: Transitions
sections.text: The transition count is the number of times the sampled level changes from sample to sample. Self-clocking codes (Manchester, RZ when the bit has a pulse) have a transition inside every bit period.

sections.heading: Source to encoder to scope
sections.text: Required connections: source.out to encoder.in and encoder.out to scope.in. Any extra wire is unexpected.

sections.heading: Reading a fault
sections.text: The engine reports missing (required wires absent) and unexpected (wires not in the required set). A missing wire breaks the data path; an unexpected wire is a hallucination that must be removed before testing.
